summary: Iteration 9 — Emergent Google Auth surface + onboarding birthdate gate + regressions. 10/10 backend tests pass. Frontend URL construction, AuthCallback hash cleanup, AuthContext race guard, and Onboarding ob-birthdate visibility for Google-only users all verified via mongo-seeded user + minted JWT.

test_results_detail.Link-by-email simulation: PASS - registered user + mongo patch adds google to auth_providers; password_hash intact; email/password login still returns 200
test_results_detail.GoogleAuthButton URL construction: PASS - built from window.location.origin, no hardcoded fallback; matches https://auth.emergentagent.com/?redirect=<origin>/app/descubrir
test_results_detail.AuthCallback with fake session_id: PASS - loader shows briefly, backend returns 401, user redirected to /login, window.location.hash cleaned to ''
test_results_detail.AuthContext race guard: PASS - with #session_id= in URL and ps_token in localStorage, AuthProvider does NOT call /auth/me (fetch spy count = 0)
test_results_detail.Onboarding step 0 ob-birthdate for Googl: PASS - visible when user.birthdate is null (mongo-seeded user + minted JWT)

critical_code_review_comments: server.py POST /auth/google/session correctly rejects missing header (400) and invalid session (401), and does server-side call to demobackend.emergentagent.com — good.
GoogleAuthButton.jsx uses window.location.origin with NO fallback — contract preserved. Header comment explicitly warns future edits.
AuthCallback.jsx clears the URL fragment via history.replaceState BEFORE the fetch, so a refresh during network latency does not retry — correct order.
AuthContext refresh() early-returns before reading ps_token when hash contains session_id — this correctly avoids the /auth/me race.

Minor: onboarding endpoint uses effective_birthdate = user.get('birthdate') or body.birthdate. If a returning Google user already completed onboarding but is somehow re-submitting with a new birthdate, the stored one wins. Acceptable but worth documenting.
server.py is now 1649 lines — recommend splitting auth (email + google) into its own router for maintainability.

google_session endpoint does not enforce rate-limiting; a valid session_id can be replayed by an attacker who steals it. Consider single-use / short-TTL enforcement (upstream Emergent may already handle this).
